Speak truth boldly, trusting that God can change any situation
Try to manage or control the situation to get the outcome you want

questions.question: Your biggest struggle in your spiritual life is:

options.text: Feeling inadequate or unqualified for what God is asking you to do
Compromising your convictions when pressured by others
Letting fear of failure stop you from stepping out in faith
Growing impatient when God's timing doesn't match your expectations
Struggling to surrender control and let God lead

questions.question: When you imagine your life five years from now, your dominant emotion is:

options.text: Sober hope — you believe change is possible but know the road will be hard
Anxiety — you worry about disappointing the people who depend on you
Dread — the obstacles between here and there feel insurmountable
Expectation — you believe God has good things ahead regardless of current circumstances
Restlessness — you want results on your terms and your timeline

results.title: The Reluctant Leader
results.description: Like Moses, you feel the weight of responsibility deeply. You see the bondage in your life and the lives of others, and you want to do something about it — but you are haunted by a sense of inadequacy. You may have tried before and failed. You may feel too old, too broken, or too disqualified. But God specializes in calling the reluctant. Your awareness of your own weakness is not a disqualification — it is the very quality that will keep you dependent on God rather than yourself. Stop waiting to feel ready. Moses was eighty years old and hiding in the desert when God called him. You have been prepared for this moment longer than you realize.
strengths: Deep empathy born from personal experience with failure and pain
Willingness to carry burdens for others even at personal cost
Genuine humility that keeps you dependent on God rather than self
Capacity for persistent intercession on behalf of others
watchFor: Using inadequacy as an excuse to avoid obedience — God has already answered your objections
Trying to deliver people in your own strength instead of God's power
Burnout from carrying responsibilities that God did not assign to you
Anger that erupts after prolonged patience — Moses struck the rock when he should have spoken

scripture.text: But he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.' Therefore I will boast all the more gladly about my weaknesses, so that Christ's power may rest on me.

results.title: The Peacekeeper
results.description: Like Aaron, your greatest gift is also your greatest vulnerability: you care deeply about people and desperately want to keep everyone happy. You are warm, relational, and often the person others turn to for comfort. But your need for approval can lead you to compromise when you should confront, to enable when you should set boundaries, and to go along with destructive behavior to avoid conflict. Your journey to freedom requires learning that love sometimes looks like a hard 'no.' The most loving thing Aaron could have done was refuse to build the calf — even if the people hated him for it. True peace is not the absence of conflict. It is the presence of truth.
strengths: Natural empathy and relational warmth that draws people in
Ability to communicate difficult truths when supported by strong leadership
Desire for unity and harmony in community
Willingness to serve in supporting roles without needing the spotlight
watchFor: Enabling destructive behavior because confrontation feels worse than complicity
Minimizing your role when things go wrong — the 'it just happened' defense
Functioning well only under strong leadership and collapsing in its absence
Confusing peace-faking with peacemaking — they are not the same

scripture.text: Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses.

results.title: The Cautious Analyst
results.description: Like the ten spies, you are perceptive, detail-oriented, and realistic about obstacles. You see problems others miss. You calculate risks others ignore. These are genuine strengths — the world needs people who count the cost. But your analytical nature becomes a cage when it focuses exclusively on what could go wrong while ignoring what God has already done. You stand at the border of your Promised Land with a detailed report of every giant, every wall, and every risk — and your report is accurate. But it is incomplete, because it leaves out the most important data point: the God who has already defeated Pharaoh, parted the sea, and sustained you through the wilderness. Add God to your analysis, and the equation changes entirely.
strengths: Ability to assess situations realistically and identify genuine obstacles
Attention to detail that helps groups avoid reckless decisions
Honest reporting that prevents unhealthy naivety
Concern for the well-being and safety of the community
watchFor: Letting realistic assessment become faithless resignation — 'we can't' replacing 'God can'
Spreading fear to others through your analysis — negativity is contagious
Defining yourself by your smallness rather than God's greatness — the 'grasshopper mentality'
Preferring familiar bondage over uncertain freedom because bondage is at least predictable

scripture.text: So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with my righteous right hand.

results.title: The Bold Believer
results.description: Like Joshua and Caleb, you have a 'different spirit.' Where others see obstacles, you see opportunities. Where others calculate risk, you calculate the faithfulness of God. Your instinct in the face of giants is not retreat but advance. This is a powerful and rare quality — and it can change the course of communities, families, and nations. But bold faith requires patience as well as courage. Joshua and Caleb waited forty years between the promise and the fulfillment. Your greatest test may not be the initial charge — it may be the long obedience between the vision and the victory. Can your faith sustain not just the battle but the wait?
strengths: Courage to stand for truth even when outnumbered and opposed
Ability to inspire others toward faith-driven action
Long-term perspective that sees beyond present circumstances
Wholehearted devotion that refuses to settle for partial obedience
watchFor: Impatience with those who process fear more slowly — not everyone has your faith temperament
Confusing boldness with recklessness — courage without wisdom is presumption
Burnout from fighting battles alone because you ran ahead of the community
Frustration during long seasons of waiting — your greatest test is the wilderness between the promise and the land

scripture.text: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the Lord your God will be with you wherever you go.

results.title: The Controller
results.description: This is the hardest result to receive, but it may be the most important. Like Pharaoh, your core struggle is control. You resist surrender — to God, to accountability, to the vulnerability that freedom requires. You may make promises during crisis that you abandon when the pressure lifts. You may acknowledge God intellectually while functionally living as your own lord. The pattern of temporary repentance followed by reversion to old behavior is Pharaoh's pattern, and it leads to a hardened heart. But here is the good news that separates you from Pharaoh: you are reading this. Pharaoh never asked for self-examination. The fact that you are willing to consider whether you have a control problem means the hardening is not yet complete. There is still time to surrender. But the window narrows with every refusal.
strengths: Strong will and determination — when redirected by God, this becomes powerful perseverance
Leadership capacity and ability to influence others toward action
Awareness of power dynamics and how systems work
Capacity for decisive action when you choose to act
watchFor: Temporary repentance driven by pain rather than genuine change of heart
Hardening your heart incrementally — each refusal makes the next one easier
Pursuing people or situations you should release — Pharaoh chased Israel to the sea
Treating God as a negotiating partner rather than the sovereign Lord who commands your obedience

scripture.text: My sacrifice, O God, is a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart you, God, will not despise.
